error_modes.label: Altitude control and level-off in the descent

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check with attention held on the navigation display, did not monitor the altimeter through the descent and did not anticipate the level-off. SP passed the cleared altitude by more than 300 feet and continued descending until IP intervened with control inputs to arrest the descent. SP did not initiate any recovery independently, and the aircraft state was not restored without assistance.
texts.1: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check that left the altimeter outside the scan for long intervals, did not lead the level-off with a timely power reduction and pitch change. Deviation from the cleared altitude reached the 300 feet limit and SP corrected only after repeated verbal prompting by IP. The recovery was late and the altitude was regained slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a cross-check that dwelled on the navigation instruments at the expense of the altimeter, allowed the vertical profile to run ahead of the intended one. Altitude deviation grew past 150 feet and reached approximately 200 to 250 feet before SP detected it. SP corrected in good time and returned to the cleared altitude without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained an active instrument cross-check that kept the altimeter in the scan throughout the descent. Altitude was held within 150 feet of the cleared and intermediate altitudes, and the level-off was led with a timely power and pitch change. Corrections were prompt and precise.
texts.4: SP flew the en-route descent with a continuous and evenly distributed cross-check, holding altitude essentially on the cleared values with negligible excursions. The level-off was anticipated and executed with no perceptible overshoot. Vertical profile control was of a standard well above the level expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within tolerance during the en-route descent, but the deviations clustered toward the outer part of the acceptable band and were consistently on the low side approaching level-off. SP corrected each time before any prompting, yet the cross-check returned to the altimeter later than desirable. SP is expected to tighten the vertical scan and lead the level-off earlier so that altitude control is centered rather than marginal.

texts_at.0: SP flew the en-route descent with the IP calling the altitude trend and talking through keeping the altimeter in the scan through the descent. This is SP's first exposure to leading a level-off from an en-route descent, and keeping the altimeter in the scan through the whole descent has not yet become a habit. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin keeping the altimeter in the scan independently through the descent, with the IP available to call any trend that is missed.
texts_at.1: SP kept the altimeter in the scan to the standard expected at this stage, letting deviation from the cleared altitude reach the 300 feet limit before correcting after repeated verbal prompting. The prompting followed an interrupted cross-check that left the altimeter outside the scan for long intervals. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to lead the level-off with a timely power reduction and pitch change rather than correcting only after repeated prompts.
texts_at.2: SP corrected in good time without IP intervention, letting altitude deviation grow past 150 feet to approximately 200 to 250 feet before returning to the cleared altitude. The cross-check is still dwelling on the navigation instruments at the expense of the altimeter before the deviation is detected. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the altimeter in the scan alongside the navigation instruments rather than letting it dwell on one at a time.
texts_at.3: SP maintained an active instrument cross-check that kept the altimeter in the scan throughout the descent on most of it, holding altitude within 150 feet with the level-off led by a timely power and pitch change. One level-off needed a slightly later lead than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to lead that level-off as promptly as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP kept the altimeter in the scan, letting deviation from the cleared altitude reach about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, before correcting. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP corrected in good time without IP intervention, letting altitude deviation grow past 150 feet to approximately 200 to 250 feet before returning to the cleared altitude. Keeping the altimeter in the scan alongside the navigation instruments, rather than letting it dwell on one at a time, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good scan integration.
texts_above.3: SP maintained an active instrument cross-check that kept the altimeter in the scan throughout the descent, with altitude held within 150 feet of the cleared and intermediate altitudes and the level-off led with a timely power and pitch change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good vertical-profile control.
texts_above.4: SP flew the en-route descent with a continuous and evenly distributed cross-check, holding altitude essentially on the cleared values with negligible excursions and the level-off anticipated and executed with no perceptible overshoot. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent cross-check distribution.

texts.0: SP, due to setting descent power without reference to the pitch attitude required for the target airspeed, allowed the airspeed to diverge and did not arrest the trend. Airspeed departed the briefed value by more than 20 KIAS and continued to increase, so IP intervened on the power lever to recover the parameter. SP did not recognize the divergence from the airspeed indicator in time.
texts.1: SP, due to a power setting that did not match the selected descent attitude, did not stabilize the airspeed at the briefed value. Airspeed deviation reached the 20 KIAS limit and was corrected only after IP called it verbally. The subsequent correction was coarse and the airspeed settled slowly.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power adjustment after establishing the descent attitude, permitted the airspeed to drift from the briefed value. The deviation exceeded 10 KIAS and reached approximately 15 KIAS before SP recognized it. SP restored the airspeed in good time with a smooth power change and without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP established the descent with a power setting and attitude matched to the briefed airspeed and held the parameter within 10 KIAS throughout. Small deviations were detected early and corrected with smooth, measured power changes. Airspeed control remained stable through the level-off.
texts.4: SP controlled airspeed with negligible deviation from the briefed descent value from entry to level-off. Power and attitude were coordinated so precisely that no corrective input larger than a small power adjustment was required. Airspeed control was of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP held airspeed within tolerance, but the values sat persistently toward the fast side of the acceptable band and the trend was not fully arrested until late in the descent. SP recognized and corrected without assistance on each occasion. SP is expected to set descent power more decisively at entry so that airspeed remains centered on the briefed value rather than close to the outer limit.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent with the IP setting power to match the descent attitude and talking through stabilizing airspeed at the briefed value. This is SP's first exposure to matching power to a chosen descent attitude, and stabilizing airspeed at entry has not yet become routine. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin matching power to the descent attitude independently at entry, with the IP available to confirm the setting.
texts_at.1: SP held airspeed to the standard expected at this stage, letting deviation reach the 20 KIAS limit before it was corrected. The correction followed the IP calling it verbally rather than SP's own match of power to the selected attitude. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match power to the descent attitude at the start of the descent rather than after a deviation has been called.
texts_at.2: SP restored airspeed in good time with a smooth power change and without IP intervention, letting deviation exceed 10 KIAS and reach approximately 15 KIAS before it was corrected. The power adjustment is still delayed after the descent attitude is established rather than made with it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to adjust power as the descent attitude is established rather than after airspeed has begun to drift.
texts_at.3: SP established the descent with a power setting and attitude matched to the briefed airspeed and held the parameter within 10 KIAS throughout on most of the descent, with small deviations detected early and corrected smoothly. One correction was slightly larger than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as measured as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP held airspeed, letting deviation reach about 20 KIAS, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP restored airspeed in good time with a smooth power change and without IP intervention, letting deviation exceed 10 KIAS and reach approximately 15 KIAS before it was corrected. Adjusting power as the descent attitude is established, rather than after airspeed has drifted, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound power-and-attitude coordination.
texts_above.3: SP established the descent with a power setting and attitude matched to the briefed airspeed and held the parameter within 10 KIAS throughout, with small deviations detected early and corrected with smooth, measured power changes and control remaining stable through the level-off. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed airspeed control.
texts_above.4: SP controlled airspeed with negligible deviation from the briefed descent value from entry to level-off, with power and attitude coordinated so precisely that no corrective input larger than a small power adjustment was required. error_modes.label: Heading and course keeping during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to uncorrected trim and inattention to the heading indicator while managing the descent, allowed a continuous drift off the assigned heading. The deviation exceeded 10 degrees and continued to grow away from the cleared track, so IP intervened to return the aircraft to heading. SP did not detect the divergence unaided.
texts.1: SP, due to bank inputs that were not held steady while the power was being adjusted, did not maintain the assigned heading during the descent. Heading deviation reached the 10 degree limit and was corrected only after IP pointed it out. The correction was overcontrolled and required a second adjustment to settle.
texts.2: SP, due to an out-of-trim condition following the power reduction, allowed the aircraft to drift off the assigned heading. The deviation passed 5 degrees and reached approximately 7 to 8 degrees before SP noticed it. SP corrected promptly with a shallow, coordinated turn and regained the assigned heading without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within 5 degrees throughout the en-route descent, including during power and configuration changes. Corrections were small, coordinated and applied as soon as a trend appeared. Directional control remained steady through the level-off.
texts.4: SP held the assigned heading essentially on value for the whole descent, with excursions that were barely perceptible on the instrument. Turns to new headings were rolled out on target without oscillation. Directional control was consistently precise.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading within tolerance, but the aircraft was allowed to wander repeatedly to one side of the assigned value before each correction. SP detected and fixed the drift without prompting, although the corrections were reactive rather than anticipatory. SP is expected to keep the aircraft trimmed after each power change so that heading is held rather than repeatedly recaptured.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent with the IP calling the heading trend and talking through retrimming after each power change. This is SP's first exposure to holding heading through power changes in a descent, and retrimming after each change has not yet been built. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to begin retrimming independently after each power change, with the IP available to call any drift that develops.
texts_at.1: SP held heading to the standard expected at this stage, letting deviation reach the 10 degree limit before it was corrected. The correction followed the IP pointing it out rather than SP's own detection of the drift. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the heading indicator in the scan while power is being adjusted rather than letting bank go unmonitored.
texts_at.2: SP corrected promptly with a shallow, coordinated turn and regained the assigned heading without IP intervention, letting deviation pass 5 degrees and reach approximately 7 to 8 degrees before it was corrected. The aircraft is still allowed to drift out of trim following the power reduction before the correction is made. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to retrim immediately after each power change so the aircraft does not drift before the correction is needed.
texts_at.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within 5 degrees throughout the en-route descent, including during power and configuration changes, on most of it, with corrections small, coordinated and applied as soon as a trend appeared. One correction needed a slightly larger input than the rest, without leaving the standard. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that correction as small as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP held heading, letting deviation reach about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP corrected promptly with a shallow, coordinated turn and regained the assigned heading without IP intervention, letting deviation pass 5 degrees and reach approximately 7 to 8 degrees before it was corrected. Retrimming immediately after each power change, rather than letting the aircraft drift first, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady directional control.
texts_above.3: SP maintained the assigned heading within 5 degrees throughout the en-route descent, including during power and configuration changes, with corrections small, coordinated and applied as soon as a trend appeared. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good heading discipline.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned heading essentially on value for the whole descent, with excursions barely perceptible on the instrument and turns to new headings rolled out on target without oscillation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding directional precision.

error_modes.label: ATC clearance compliance and readback for the descent

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete readback that left the assigned descent altitude unconfirmed, began the en-route descent to an altitude that was not the one cleared by ATC. SP did not comply with the ATC instruction and did not query the controller when the instruction was unclear. IP intervened, took the radios and stopped the descent before the aircraft continued more than 300 ft below the cleared level.
texts.1: SP, due to a readback that omitted the altitude restriction issued with the clearance, did not comply fully with the ATC descent instruction. SP began the descent late and to the wrong intermediate level, and complied only after IP restated the clearance verbally. The resulting altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit before the correct profile was resumed.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried readback made while still adjusting the descent power, misheard part of the ATC instruction. SP started the descent with the wrong initial rate but recognized the discrepancy, requested confirmation from the controller on SP's own initiative and complied correctly. The resulting altitude deviation stayed between 150 and 300 feet and no IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP read back the descent clearance completely and accurately, including the assigned altitude and any restriction, and complied with the ATC instruction without delay. Radio work did not interfere with aircraft control and all parameters remained within tolerance during the exchange. Coordination with the controller was clear and standard.
texts.4: SP handled the ATC descent clearance with a concise, complete readback and immediate, exact compliance, while flight parameters remained essentially unaffected. SP anticipated the clearance and was prepared for the descent before it was issued. Radio discipline and compliance were of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP complied with the ATC descent clearance and the readback contained all mandatory elements, but the phraseology was hesitant and the compliance action followed the instruction later than expected. Parameters stayed within tolerance during the radio work. SP is expected to consolidate standard phraseology so that clearances are read back and acted upon without hesitation.

texts_at.0: SP worked the ATC descent clearance with the IP confirming the assigned altitude and any restriction in the readback. This is SP's first exposure to a full descent-clearance readback under workload, and confirming every element has not yet become routine. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin confirming every element of the clearance independently in the readback, with the IP available to confirm the altitude.
texts_at.1: SP complied with the ATC descent clearance to the standard expected at this stage, with the altitude deviation reaching the 300 feet limit before the correct profile was resumed. The resumption followed the IP restating the clearance verbally rather than SP's own complete readback. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to read back the altitude restriction as issued rather than omitting it and correcting after IP intervenes.
texts_at.2: SP requested confirmation from the controller on SP's own initiative, letting the resulting altitude deviation stay between 150 and 300 feet before complying correctly. The readback is still made in a hurry while the descent power is still being adjusted rather than after it settles. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to complete the power adjustment before transmitting the readback so it is not made mid-task.
texts_at.3: SP read back the descent clearance completely and accurately, including the assigned altitude and any restriction, and complied with the ATC instruction without delay on most of the descent, with radio work not interfering with aircraft control. One exchange needed a brief follow-up, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to make that exchange as clean as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP complied with the ATC descent clearance, with the altitude deviation reaching about 300 feet, at the tolerance limit, before the correct profile was resumed. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP requested confirmation from the controller on SP's own initiative, letting the resulting altitude deviation stay between 150 and 300 feet before complying correctly. Completing the power adjustment before transmitting the readback, rather than mid-task, would keep that deviation smaller. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable clearance handling.
texts_above.3: SP read back the descent clearance completely and accurately, including the assigned altitude and any restriction, and complied with the ATC instruction without delay, with radio work not interfering with aircraft control and all parameters remaining within tolerance during the exchange. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good radio discipline.
texts_above.4: SP handled the ATC descent clearance with a concise, complete readback and immediate, exact compliance, while flight parameters remained essentially unaffected, anticipating the clearance and being prepared for the descent before it was issued. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary clearance anticipation.

error_modes.label: Routing and altitude restrictions from MAIP and approach manuals

texts.0: SP, due to not having reviewed the published route and altitude restrictions for the arrival before commencing the descent, violated a published minimum altitude segment. SP descended below the published level by more than 300 feet and showed no awareness of the restriction. IP intervened to level the aircraft and to restore the published profile.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the MAIP and approach manual data, did not respect a published altitude restriction on the arrival. SP arrived at the restriction point at the 300 feet limit off the published altitude and corrected only after IP identified the restriction verbally. The published routing was regained late.
texts.2: SP, due to referring to the published restrictions only after the descent had begun, planned the descent rate against the wrong crossing point. Altitude at the restriction point was between 150 and 300 feet off the published value, but SP identified the error, adjusted the descent rate and complied at the following segment without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP flew the en-route descent within the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. Crossing altitudes were planned before commencing the descent and met within 150 feet. No restriction was violated at any point.
texts.4: SP applied the published routing and altitude restrictions with full accuracy, crossing every constraint point essentially on the published value. The descent rate was planned in advance so that no late adjustment was needed. Knowledge and application of the published data were of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP respected all published routing and altitude restrictions, but crossing altitudes were met with little margin and the descent rate was adjusted late at more than one segment. No restriction was violated and no assistance was needed. SP is expected to plan the descent profile earlier so that published constraints are met with a comfortable margin rather than marginally.

texts_at.0: SP flew the routing with the IP calling the published restrictions and talking through reviewing MAIP and the approach manual before the descent. This is SP's first exposure to reviewing published altitude restrictions before a descent, and completing that review before commencing has not yet been built. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin completing the review independently before commencing the descent, with the IP available to confirm each restriction.
texts_at.1: SP respected published routing and altitude restrictions to the standard expected at this stage, arriving at the restriction point at the 300 feet limit before it was corrected. The correction followed the IP identifying the restriction verbally rather than SP's own review of the MAIP data. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the review of MAIP and approach manual data before commencing the descent rather than referring to it after arriving at a restriction.
texts_at.2: SP identified the error, adjusted the descent rate and complied at the following segment without IP intervention, with altitude at the restriction point between 150 and 300 feet off the published value. The published restrictions are still referred to only after the descent has begun rather than before it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to refer to the published restrictions before the descent begins so the rate is planned against the correct crossing point from the start.
texts_at.3: SP flew the en-route descent within the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals on most of it, with crossing altitudes planned before commencing the descent and met within 150 feet. One crossing altitude was met with a slightly narrower margin, without a restriction being violated. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that margin as comfortable as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP respected published routing and altitude restrictions, arriving at the restriction point at about 300 feet off, at the tolerance limit, before it was corrected. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP identified the error, adjusted the descent rate and complied at the following segment without IP intervention, with altitude at the restriction point between 150 and 300 feet off the published value. Referring to the published restrictions before the descent begins, rather than after, would keep that margin wider from the start. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent restriction planning.
texts_above.3: SP flew the en-route descent within the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals, with crossing altitudes planned before commencing the descent and met within 150 feet, no restriction violated at any point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined descent planning.
texts_above.4: SP applied the published routing and altitude restrictions with full accuracy, crossing every constraint point essentially on the published value with the descent rate planned in advance so no late adjustment was needed. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless restriction accuracy.

error_modes.label: Standardized descent procedure and sequence without IP intervention

texts.0: SP, due to not applying the descent sequence described in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, omitted the descent checks and configured the aircraft out of order. The omissions accumulated and the aircraft was left more than 300 feet off the assigned altitude in a state that required IP to take control and re-establish the correct procedure. SP did not execute the descent without mistakes or without IP intervention.
texts.1: SP, due to an unrehearsed descent flow, performed the required actions out of the standardized sequence and omitted one item until reminded. SP completed the procedure only after IP prompted each remaining step verbally. Flight parameters reached the outer limits, with altitude at 300 feet off the assigned value, while SP was catching up with the sequence.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the descent checks after rather than before initiating the descent, executed part of the sequence out of order. SP recognized the omission unaided, went back and completed the missing items correctly. Parameters remained between the code 3 and code 1 bands, with altitude no worse than 250 feet off, and IP did not intervene.
texts.3: SP executed the en-route descent according to the standardized procedures of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, in the correct sequence and without mistakes. Descent checks were completed before entering the descent and no item was omitted. No IP intervention was required at any stage.
texts.4: SP flew the en-route descent to a standardized flow that was complete, correctly ordered and unhurried, with every check accomplished ahead of the point where it was needed. The procedure was executed flawlessly and left ample capacity for aircraft control and navigation. Procedural execution was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP executed the descent procedure correctly and in sequence, but the flow was slow and each step was completed close to the point at which it was needed. No item was omitted and no prompting was required. SP is expected to rehearse the descent flow so that the procedure is completed with margin rather than at the last available moment.

texts_at.0: SP worked the descent checks with the IP talking through the standardized sequence and completing each item in order. This is SP's first exposure to a rehearsed descent flow, and completing the standardized sequence in order under workload has not yet been built. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin rehearsing the standardized sequence independently, with the IP available to confirm each step.
texts_at.1: SP executed the descent sequence to the standard expected at this stage, with altitude reaching 300 feet off the assigned value while SP caught up with the sequence. The completion followed IP prompting each remaining step verbally rather than SP's own rehearsal of the flow. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to rehearse the standardized descent sequence so it is not performed out of order under workload.
texts_at.2: SP recognized the omission unaided, went back and completed the missing items correctly, with parameters remaining between the code 3 and code 1 bands and altitude no worse than 250 feet off. The descent checks are still started after rather than before initiating the descent. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the descent checks before initiating the descent rather than after it has begun.
texts_at.3: SP executed the en-route descent according to the standardized procedures of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, in the correct sequence and without mistakes, on most of the descent, with descent checks completed before entering the descent and no item omitted. One item was completed a little later than the rest, without a mistake resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to complete that item as promptly as the rest of the sequence.

texts_above.1: SP executed the descent sequence, with altitude reaching about 300 feet off the assigned value while catching up with the sequence, at the tolerance limit. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the omission unaided, went back and completed the missing items correctly, with parameters remaining between the code 3 and code 1 bands and altitude no worse than 250 feet off. Starting the descent checks before initiating the descent, rather than after, would remove that omission entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured procedural recovery.
texts_above.3: SP executed the en-route descent according to the standardized procedures of the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3, in the correct sequence and without mistakes, with descent checks completed before entering the descent and no item omitted or IP intervention required. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise procedural execution.
texts_above.4: SP flew the en-route descent to a standardized flow that was complete, correctly ordered and unhurried, with every check accomplished ahead of the point where it was needed and ample capacity left for aircraft control and navigation. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate procedural flow.

error_modes.label: Radio navigation aid use and orientation during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of awareness of the aircraft position relative to the navigation facility, did not tune, identify or correctly interpret the radio aid used for the en-route descent. SP became disoriented as to position along the route and continued the descent on an incorrect track, with the heading deviation passing 10 degrees from the cleared track. IP intervened to re-establish orientation and to return the aircraft to the cleared routing.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete picture of the aircraft position relative to the facility, did not use the radio aid to maintain orientation during the descent. SP required IP to state the position and the required track before continuing. The resulting heading deviation reached the 10 degree limit and the track was regained only after the verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed update of the navigation picture after the descent was commenced, misread the position relative to the facility. SP identified the error from the raw data unaided, re-established orientation and returned to the correct track. Heading deviation stayed between 5 and 10 degrees and no IP intervention was needed.
texts.3: SP tuned and identified the radio aids correctly and used them to maintain accurate orientation throughout the en-route descent. Position relative to the facility was known at all times and the aircraft was flown on the cleared track within 5 degrees. SP demonstrated a clear navigation picture without assistance.
texts.4: SP used the radio navigation aids with full accuracy, maintaining an unbroken awareness of position along the route and of the distance and altitude required at each point. Orientation was never in doubt and SP could state the required action to reach the destination or the alternate at any moment. Navigation awareness was of a very high standard.
texts.marginal: SP maintained orientation with the radio aids and flew the cleared track within tolerance, but the navigation picture was rebuilt by repeated checks rather than held continuously. SP answered position questions correctly, though after a noticeable delay. SP is expected to keep the navigation picture updated throughout the descent so that orientation is immediate rather than reconstructed.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent with the IP stating aircraft position relative to the facility and talking through building the navigation picture from the radio aids. This is SP's first exposure to building a continuous navigation picture from the radio aids, and holding that picture through the descent has not yet been built. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin building the navigation picture independently from the radio aids, with the IP available to confirm the position.
texts_at.1: SP used the radio aid to hold orientation to the standard expected at this stage, letting the heading deviation reach the 10 degree limit before the track was regained. The regain followed IP stating the position and the required track rather than SP's own picture of position relative to the facility. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to build a complete picture of position relative to the facility before it is needed, not reconstruct it once the IP states it.
texts_at.2: SP identified the error from the raw data unaided, letting heading deviation stay between 5 and 10 degrees before orientation was re-established and the correct track regained. The navigation picture is still updated late after the descent has been commenced rather than continuously through it. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to update the navigation picture continuously through the descent rather than only after a position question arises.
texts_at.3: SP tuned and identified the radio aids correctly and used them to maintain accurate orientation throughout the en-route descent on most of it, with position relative to the facility known at all times and the aircraft flown on the cleared track within 5 degrees. One update lagged briefly behind the rest, without a deviation resulting. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to keep that update as current as the rest of the descent.

texts_above.1: SP used the radio aid to hold orientation, letting the heading deviation reach about 10 degrees, at the tolerance limit, before the track was regained. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP identified the error from the raw data unaided, letting heading deviation stay between 5 and 10 degrees before orientation was re-established and the correct track regained. Updating the navigation picture continuously through the descent, rather than only when a question arises, would keep that deviation smaller. error_modes.label: Airspeed restriction below 10,000 feet MSL during the descent

texts.0: SP, due to steepening the gradient to make a published altitude restriction without adjusting airspeed for it, exceeded 250 KIAS below 10,000 feet MSL and made no power reduction to recover the limit. The excursion continued and airspeed reached more than 20 KIAS above the descent speed while the profile was flown steeply. IP intervened on the power lever and speed brake to bring the aircraft back within limits.
texts.1: SP, due to a steepened descent gradient flown without a matching power reduction, accelerated toward 250 KIAS below 10,000 feet MSL. SP retarded the power only after IP called the speed, and the airspeed excursion reached the 20 KIAS limit from the descent speed. The recovery required speed brake and a marked pitch change.
texts.2: SP, due to increasing the descent gradient without anticipating the acceleration that follows, allowed airspeed to rise as the aircraft approached 10,000 feet MSL. SP detected the trend before the restriction applied, used power and speed brake in good time and kept the airspeed error between 10 and 20 KIAS. The 250 KIAS limit was not exceeded and no IP input was needed.
texts.3: SP managed airspeed against the 250 KIAS restriction below 10,000 feet MSL, adjusting power and speed brake as the gradient was changed to meet the published restrictions. Airspeed stayed within 10 KIAS of the descent speed and the limit was respected with margin. Adjustments were smooth and anticipatory.
texts.4: SP anticipated the acceleration associated with each gradient change and kept airspeed comfortably clear of the 250 KIAS restriction below 10,000 feet MSL. Airspeed held essentially on the descent value with negligible variation and speed brake was used sparingly and precisely. Speed control against the published restriction was well above the standard expected.
texts.marginal: SP remained below 250 KIAS through the lower part of the descent, but airspeed was allowed to sit close to the restriction and speed brake had to be held to contain it. All values remained within tolerance with a clear tendency toward the fast side. SP is expected to set the gradient and power so that the margin below the restriction is kept without continuous speed brake use.

texts_at.0: SP flew the descent with the IP calling the approaching restricted altitude and talking through matching a power reduction to the steepened gradient. error_modes.label: Planning the descent to allow unhurried deceleration and configuration before the FAF

texts.0: SP, due to not planning the descent so the aircraft could be configured before the FAF, arrived at the approach segment high and fast with the whole deceleration still to be made. The attempt to lose altitude and speed together left the aircraft more than 300 feet from the required altitude and more than 20 KIAS from the required speed. IP intervened to configure the aircraft and stabilize the approach.
texts.1: SP, due to a descent profile that left no allowance for deceleration before the FAF, delayed the speed reduction until the final part of the descent. The deceleration was hurried, altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit and airspeed reached the 20 KIAS limit before SP acted on IP prompting. Configuration was completed late.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the deceleration later than the planned profile allowed, compressed the transition from descent speed to approach speed. SP recognized the compression, reduced power in good time and completed the configuration with altitude between 150 and 300 feet and airspeed between 10 and 20 KIAS of the required values. The approach was flown without IP intervention.
texts.3: SP planned the descent so that deceleration and configuration were completed before the FAF without haste. Altitude was within 150 feet and airspeed within 10 KIAS at the point of configuration, and the power reduction was smooth. The transition into the approach was orderly.
texts.4: SP planned the descent so that the aircraft was decelerated and configured well before the FAF with no compression at any stage. Altitude and airspeed at configuration were essentially on the required values and the transition into the approach was seamless. Descent planning for the approach was of an exemplary standard.
texts.marginal: SP was configured before the FAF, but the deceleration was begun late and had to be completed with a rapid power reduction. All parameters stayed within tolerance, with airspeed on the fast side until shortly before configuration. SP is expected to plan the descent so that the speed reduction begins early enough for an unhurried configuration.

texts_at.0: SP planned the descent with the IP talking through beginning the speed reduction early enough for an unhurried configuration before the FAF.
